{{Short description|Continuous, position-preserving mapping from a topological space into a subspace}}
In [[topology]], a '''retraction''' is a [[continuous mapping]] from a [[topological space]] into a [[Subspace topology|subspace]] that preserves the position of all points in that subspace.<ref>Borsuk (1931).</ref> The subspace is then called a '''retract''' of the original space. A '''deformation retraction''' is a mapping that captures the idea of ''continuously shrinking'' a space into a subspace.

An '''absolute neighborhood retract''' ('''ANR''') is a particularly [[well-behaved]] type of topological space. For example, every [[topological manifold]] is an ANR. Every ANR has the [[homotopy type]] of a very simple topological space, a [[CW complex]].

== Definitions ==

=== Retract ===
Let ''X'' be a topological space and ''A'' a subspace of ''X''. Then a continuous map
:<math>r\colon X \to A</math>

is a '''retraction''' if the [[function (mathematics)#Restrictions and extensions|restriction]] of ''r'' to ''A'' is the [[Identity function|identity map]] on ''A''; that is, <math display="inline">r(a) = a</math> for all ''a'' in ''A''. Equivalently, denoting by

:<math>\iota\colon A \hookrightarrow X</math>
the [[Inclusion map|inclusion]], a retraction is a continuous map ''r'' such that
:<math>r \circ \iota = \operatorname{id}_A,</math>
that is, the composition of ''r'' with the inclusion is the identity of ''A''. Note that, by definition, a retraction maps ''X'' [[onto]] ''A''. A subspace ''A'' is called a '''retract''' of ''X'' if such a retraction exists. For instance, any non-empty space retracts to a point in the obvious way (any constant map yields a retraction). If ''X'' is [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]], then ''A'' must be a [[closed subset]] of ''X''.

If <math display="inline">r: X \to A</math> is a retraction, then the composition <math>\iota \circ r</math> is an [[idempotent]] continuous map from ''X'' to ''X''. Conversely, given any idempotent continuous map <math display="inline">s: X \to X,</math> we obtain a retraction onto the image of ''s'' by restricting the [[codomain]].

=== Deformation retract and strong deformation retract===
A continuous map
:<math>F\colon X \times [0, 1] \to X </math>
is a ''deformation retraction'' of a space ''X'' onto a subspace ''A'' if, for every ''x'' in ''X'' and ''a'' in ''A'',
:<math> F(x,0) = x, \quad F(x,1) \in A ,\quad \mbox{and} \quad F(a,1) = a.</math>
In other words, a deformation retraction is a [[homotopy]] between a retraction (strictly, between its composition with the inclusion) and the identity map on ''X''. The subspace ''A'' is called a '''deformation retract''' of ''X''. A deformation retraction is a special case of a [[homotopy equivalence]].

A retract need not be a deformation retract. For instance, having a single point as a deformation retract of a space ''X'' would imply that ''X'' is [[path connected]] (and in fact that ''X'' is [[contractible space|contractible]]).

''Note:'' An equivalent definition of deformation retraction is the following. A continuous map <math display="inline">r: X \to A</math> is itself called a deformation retraction if it is a retraction and its composition with the inclusion is homotopic to the identity map on ''X''. In this language, a deformation retraction still carries with it a homotopy between the identity map on ''X'' and itself, but we refer to the map <math display="inline">r</math> rather than the homotopy as a deformation retraction.

If, in the definition of a deformation retraction, we add the requirement that
:<math>F(a,t) = a</math>
for all ''t'' in [0, 1] and ''a'' in ''A'', then ''F'' is called a '''strong deformation retraction'''. In other words, a strong deformation retraction leaves points in ''A'' fixed throughout the homotopy. (Some authors, such as [[Allen Hatcher|Hatcher]], take this as the definition of deformation retraction.)

As an example, the [[n-sphere|''n''-sphere]] ''<math display="inline">S^{n}</math>'' is a strong deformation retract of <math display="inline">\reals^{n+1} \backslash \{0\};</math> as strong deformation retraction one can choose the map

:<math>F(x,t)=(1-t)x+t{x\over \|x\|}.</math>

Note that the condition of being a strong deformation retract is ''strictly [[Glossary_of_mathematical_jargon#strong|stronger]]'' than being a deformation retract. For instance, let ''X'' be the [[closed infinite broom]]. It is the subspace of <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math> consisting of closed line segments connecting the origin and the point <math>(1,1/n)</math> for ''n'' a positive integer, together with the closed line segment connecting the origin with <math>(0,1)</math>. Let X have the subspace topology inherited from the [[Euclidean topology]] on <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math>. Now let ''A'' be the subspace of ''X'' consisting of the line segment connecting the origin with <math>(1,0)</math>. Then ''A'' is a deformation retract of ''X'' but not a strong deformation retract of ''X''.<ref>{{cite book|last=Weintraub|first=Steven H.|title=Fundamentals of Algebraic Topology|series=[[Graduate Texts in Mathematics]]|volume=270|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]]|page=20}}</ref>

===Cofibration and neighborhood deformation retract===
A map ''f'': ''A'' → ''X'' of topological spaces is a ([[Witold Hurewicz|Hurewicz]]) '''[[cofibration]]''' if it has the [[homotopy extension property]] for maps to any space. This is one of the central concepts of [[homotopy theory]]. A cofibration ''f'' is always injective, in fact a [[homeomorphism]] to its image.<ref>Hatcher (2002), Proposition 4H.1.</ref> If ''X'' is Hausdorff (or a [[compactly generated space|compactly generated]] [[weak Hausdorff space]]), then the image of a cofibration ''f'' is closed in ''X''.

Among all closed inclusions, cofibrations can be characterized as follows. The inclusion of a closed subspace ''A'' in a space ''X'' is a cofibration if and only if ''A'' is a '''neighborhood deformation retract''' of ''X'', meaning that there is a continuous map <math>u: X \rightarrow [0, 1]</math> with <math display="inline">A = u^{-1}\!\left(0\right)</math> and a homotopy <math display="inline">H: X \times [0, 1] \rightarrow X</math> such that <math display="inline">H(x,0) = x</math> for all <math>x \in X,</math> <math>H(a,t) = a</math> for all <math>a \in A</math> and <math>t \in [0, 1],</math> and <math display="inline">H\left(x,1\right) \in A</math> if <math>u(x) < 1</math>.<ref>Puppe (1967), Satz 1.</ref>

For example, the inclusion of a subcomplex in a CW complex is a cofibration.

==Properties==
* One basic property of a retract ''A'' of ''X'' (with retraction <math display="inline">r: X \to A</math>) is that every continuous map <math display="inline">f: A \rightarrow Y</math> has at least one extension <math display="inline">g: X \rightarrow Y,</math> namely <math display="inline">g = f \circ r</math>.
* If a subspace is a retract of a space, then the inclusion induces an injection between fundamental groups.
* Deformation retraction is a particular case of homotopy equivalence. In fact, two spaces are homotopy equivalent [[if and only if]] they are both homeomorphic to deformation retracts of a single larger space.
* Any topological space that deformation retracts to a point is contractible and vice versa. However, there exist contractible spaces that do not strongly deformation retract to a point.<ref>Hatcher (2002), Exercise 0.6.</ref>

==No-retraction theorem==
The [[boundary (topology)|boundary]] of the [[N-ball|''n''-dimensional ball]], that is, the (''n''−1)-sphere, is not a retract of the ball. (See {{Section link|Brouwer fixed-point theorem|A proof using homology or cohomology}}.)

==Absolute neighborhood retract (ANR)==
{{main|Absolute neighborhood retract}}
A closed subset <math display="inline">X</math> of a topological space <math display="inline">Y</math> is called a '''neighborhood retract''' of <math display="inline">Y</math> if <math display="inline">X</math> is a retract of some open subset of <math display="inline">Y</math> that contains <math display="inline">X</math>.

Let <math>\mathcal{C}</math> be a class of topological spaces, closed under homeomorphisms and passage to closed subsets. Following [[Karol Borsuk|Borsuk]] (starting in 1931), a space ''<math display="inline">X</math>'' is called an '''absolute retract''' for the class <math>\mathcal{C}</math>, written <math display="inline">\operatorname{AR} \left(\mathcal{C}\right),</math> if ''<math display="inline">X</math>'' is in <math>\mathcal{C}</math> and whenever ''<math display="inline">X</math>'' is a closed subset of a space  <math display="inline">Y</math> in <math>\mathcal{C}</math>, <math display="inline">X</math> is a retract of <math display="inline">Y</math>. A space <math display="inline">X</math> is an '''absolute neighborhood retract''' for the class <math>\mathcal{C}</math>, written <math display="inline">\operatorname{ANR} \left(\mathcal{C}\right),</math> if <math display="inline">X</math> is in <math>\mathcal{C}</math> and whenever <math display="inline">X</math> is a closed subset of a space <math display="inline">Y</math> in <math>\mathcal{C}</math>, <math display="inline">X</math> is a neighborhood retract of <math display="inline">Y</math>.

Various classes <math>\mathcal{C}</math> such as [[normal space]]s have been considered in this definition, but the class <math>\mathcal{M}</math> of [[metrizable space]]s has been found to give the most satisfactory theory. For that reason, the notations AR and ANR by themselves are used in this article to mean <math>\operatorname {AR} \left({\mathcal {M}}\right)</math> and <math>\operatorname {ANR} \left({\mathcal {M}}\right)</math>.<ref>Mardešiċ (1999), p. 242.</ref>

A metrizable space is an AR if and only if it is contractible and an ANR.<ref>Hu (1965), Proposition II.7.2.</ref> By [[James Dugundji|Dugundji]], every locally convex metrizable [[topological vector space]] <math display="inline">V</math> is an AR; more generally, every nonempty [[convex set|convex subset]] of such a vector space <math display="inline">V</math> is an AR.<ref>Hu (1965), Corollary II.14.2 and Theorem II.3.1.</ref> For example, any [[normed vector space]] ([[complete metric space|complete]] or not) is an AR. More concretely, Euclidean space <math display="inline">\reals^{n},</math> the [[unit cube]] <math display="inline">I^{n},</math>and the [[Hilbert cube]] <math display="inline">I^{\omega}</math> are ARs.

ANRs form a remarkable class of "[[Well behaved|well-behaved]]" topological spaces. Among their properties are:
*Every open subset of an ANR is an ANR. 
*By [[Olof Hanner|Hanner]], a metrizable space that has an [[open cover]] by ANRs is an ANR.<ref>Hu (1965), Theorem III.8.1.</ref> (That is, being an ANR is a '''[[local property]]''' for metrizable spaces.) It follows that every topological manifold is an ANR. For example, the sphere ''<math display="inline">S^{n}</math>'' is an ANR but not an AR (because it is not contractible). In infinite dimensions, Hanner's theorem implies that every Hilbert cube manifold as well as the (rather different, for example not [[locally compact space|locally compact]]) [[Hilbert manifold]]s and [[Banach manifold]]s are ANRs.
*Every locally finite [[CW complex]] is an ANR.<ref>Mardešiċ (1999), p. 245.</ref> An arbitrary CW complex need not be metrizable, but every CW complex has the homotopy type of an ANR (which is metrizable, by definition).<ref>Fritsch & Piccinini (1990), Theorem 5.2.1.</ref>
*Every ANR ''X'' is '''[[locally contractible]]''' in the sense that for every open neighborhood <math display="inline">U</math> of a point <math display="inline">x</math> in <math display="inline">X</math>, there is an open neighborhood <math display="inline">V</math> of <math display="inline">x</math> contained in <math display="inline">U</math> such that the inclusion <math display="inline">V \hookrightarrow U</math> is homotopic to a [[constant map]]. A [[covering dimension|finite-dimensional]] metrizable space is an ANR if and only if it is locally contractible in this sense.<ref>Hu (1965), Theorem V.7.1.</ref> For example, the [[Cantor set]] is a [[compact space|compact]] subset of the real line that is not an ANR, since it is not even [[locally connected]].
*Counterexamples: Borsuk found a compact subset of <math display="inline">\reals^{3}</math> that is an ANR but not strictly locally contractible.<ref>Borsuk (1967), section IV.4.</ref> (A space is '''strictly locally contractible''' if every open neighborhood <math display="inline">U</math> of each point <math display="inline">x</math> contains a contractible open neighborhood of <math display="inline">x</math>.) Borsuk also found a compact subset of the Hilbert cube that is locally contractible (as defined above) but not an ANR.<ref>Borsuk (1967), Theorem V.11.1.</ref>
*Every ANR has the homotopy type of a CW complex, by [[J. H. C. Whitehead|Whitehead]] and [[John Milnor|Milnor]].<ref>Fritsch & Piccinini (1990), Theorem 5.2.1.</ref> Moreover, a locally compact ANR has the homotopy type of a locally finite CW complex; and, by West, a compact ANR has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex.<ref>West (2004), p. 119.</ref> In this sense, ANRs avoid all the homotopy-theoretic pathologies of arbitrary topological spaces. For example, the [[Whitehead theorem]] holds for ANRs: a map of ANRs that induces an isomorphism on [[homotopy group]]s (for all choices of base point) is a homotopy equivalence. Since ANRs include topological manifolds, Hilbert cube manifolds, Banach manifolds, and so on, these results apply to a large class of spaces.
*Many [[mapping space]]s are ANRs. In particular, let ''Y'' be an ANR with a closed subspace ''A'' that is an ANR, and let ''X'' be any compact metrizable space with a closed subspace ''B''. Then the space <math display="inline">\left(Y, A\right)^{\left(X, B\right)}</math> of maps of [[topological pair|pairs]] <math display="inline">\left(X, B\right) \rightarrow \left(Y, A\right)</math> (with the [[compact-open topology]] on the [[Function space|mapping space]]) is an ANR.<ref>Hu (1965), Theorem VI.3.1 and Remark VI.2.3.</ref> It follows, for example, that the [[loop space]] of any CW complex has the homotopy type of a CW complex.
*By Cauty, a metrizable space <math display="inline">X</math> is an ANR if and only if every open subset of <math display="inline">X</math> has the homotopy type of a CW complex.<ref>Cauty (1994), Fund. Math. 144: 11–22.</ref>
*By Cauty, there is a [[topological vector space#Topological structure|metric linear space]] ''<math display="inline">V</math>'' (meaning a topological vector space with a [[Translation invariant|translation-invariant]] metric) that is not an AR. One can take <math display="inline">V</math> to be [[separable space|separable]] and an [[F-space]] (that is, a complete metric linear space).<ref>Cauty (1994), Fund. Math. 146: 85–99.</ref> (By Dugundji's theorem above, <math display="inline">V</math> cannot be locally convex.) Since <math display="inline">V</math> is contractible and not an AR, it is also not an ANR. By Cauty's theorem above, <math display="inline">V</math> has an open subset <math display="inline">U</math> that is not homotopy equivalent to a CW complex. Thus there is a metrizable space <math display="inline">U</math> that is strictly locally contractible but is not homotopy equivalent to a CW complex. It is not known whether a compact (or locally compact) metrizable space that is strictly locally contractible must be an ANR.
